content.comment:
We thank all the reviewers for their effort.

While most reviewers liked the main idea of the paper, they requested several changes that probably cannot be addressed within the scope of a rebuttal. We will revise and resubmit.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper claims that "window projection features are all you need for time series anomaly detection", as given in its title. To this end, empirical analysis is conducted, supported by some theoretical insights.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
The claim "... are all you need..." is clearly presented and empirical analysis as well as theoretical insight allow to support the claim.

Weaknesses:
The paper relies essentially on empirical analysis, including some theoretical insights (density estimation and central limit theorem) that do not provide much in-depth analysis.

This contributions of this paper may not be of great interest to a large number of researchers.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper relies essentially on demonstrating the claim given in the title, mainly with an empirical analysis and some theoretical insights, which is the main originality of this work. To this end, the presentation is clear.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper clearly presents the method. While the paper is roughly based on some empirical analysis, the authors did provide some theoretical insights that allow to alleviate the experimental results.

While discrete projections have been investigated by researchers for a while, it seems to me that the novelty is the new theoretical insights, with the connections to density estimation and the central limit theorem.

There are many spelling and grammatical errors, such as "aa Gaussian estimator", "will often be be more effective", "The training set consist of", "We presents a comparison",  "increases the expressively but increase", "tradeoff between peformance", "estimate the of each"

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper present a simple but effective method for time series anomaly detection via using window projection features. The empirical analysis show some interesting conclusion that the features are sufficiently expressive for discriminating anomalies, but current one-class
classification methods are unable to use them effectively to detect anomalies. Given this, this work propose to estimate the probability density of the sample means motivated by the central limit theorem. Despite its simplicity, the proposed method outperforms the state-of-the-art in diverse settings.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:

1. The proposed window projection features and the averaging features strategies are simple but effective. Experimental results also demonstrate improvement on various anomaly detection tasks.

2. The paper is well-organized, and the writing is easy to follow. It presents the motivation from both the empirical and theoretical analysis perspectives, which give a clear justification for the proposed method.


Cons: 

1. The proposed method includes some hand-crafted processes, like the number of bins, which might limit its applicability.

2. The strategy of averaging features across adjacent windows is effective and relies on the assumption that anomalies occupy a duration of time.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper studies projection methods and the problem of detecting anomalies in time series. In particular, the paper claims that simple projections (capturing sliding windows) of the data work sufficiently well when properly integrated with a principled density estimation technique. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate the potential of the proposed methodology.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths

1. Time-series anomaly detection is an important and timely problem
2. Projection methods are not well-studied in this area so a study is well motivated
3. Sufficient experimental results to support claims in the paper

Weaknesses

1. Missing recent advances in the area with new benchmarks and new evaluation measures
2. Missing comparisons with state of the art methodologies, outside of the projection literature
3. Lack of technical depth - more advanced representation learning/projection solutions already exist that could improve even more the current solution

Comments

Despite a solid effort in demonstrating the impact of projections for this task, the paper has omitted many recent advances in the area, which significantly decreases the impact of this work

1) TSB-UAD is a new benchmark in that space. An extensive evaluation using the proposed datasets and baselines is necessary to understand if the proposed solution advances the state of the art

"Tsb-uad: an end-to-end benchmark suite for univariate time-series anomaly detection." Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment 15.8 (2022): 1697-1711.

2) VUS is a new evaluation measure in this area, which should be used as well considering several flaws of the evaluation measures traditionally used in this area

"Volume under the surface: a new accuracy evaluation measure for time-series anomaly detection." Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment 15.11 (2022): 2774-2787.

3) Representation learning techniques for time-series data are well studied. For example, GRAIL can use advanced specialized kernels for time series that outperform gaussian kernels/assumptions for multiple tasks. 

"Grail: efficient time-series representation learning." Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment 12.11 (2019): 1762-1777.

The paper seems to have omitted important works outside of the ML venues, which solve relevant problems. Importantly, the current work demonstrates the impact of projections, but it does not show if these methods achieve state-of-the-art results. Without a proper comparison on the recent comprehensive benchmark and new evaluation measures, it becomes difficult to understand the true potential of the current work.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity is sufficient. However, novelty is somewhat low considering the lack of technical depth as well as omitted baselines/datasets/evaluation solutions.

Code is provided to help with reproducibility efforts
content.summary_of_the_review: I believe the work can benefit from comparisons with works such as GRAIL/RWS and other approaches in that area. A stronger evaluation using the new benchmarks and evaluation measures would significantly strengthen this work to understand the true potential of the proposed solution.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes an anomaly detector for time series based on features computed by projecting windows of time series. The features are computed for different strides (or scales) and then averaged for the whole time series. The anomaly score is then based on the likelihood of a time series computed assuming a Gaussian distribution fitted for a set of time series. Despite the simplicity of the method, it achieves great results in practise.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**:

* Simple yet effective (as shown empirically) method
* Inviting text flow with the motivational empirical observations followed by formalisation of the method

**Weaknesses**:

* The main weakness of the paper is that it is unpolished. It seems like it needs a several rounds of edits before it is ready. 
* Ablations section represent hyperparameter tuning rather than ablation. And its’ setup is optimistic, since the same data is used to tune parameters as the data is then used for presenting the results.
* The actual ablation which is missing would be to check whether binning the raw data would give any advances. In general, I am missing intuition behind projected features. The paper does attempt to explain the average, but the whole quantized projection thing would be great to grasp more why it may be a good idea to use (on top of the empirical evidence provided).

Details:
1. Arguable statements:
    * Introduction, first paragraph. “no anomalies are seen in training” – it is an assumption that is not always true. It is actually makes a problem a little bit easier if one has a luxury of being sure that the training data is free from anomalies. One may have just unlabelled data which may or may not contain anomalies. In fact the authors contradict to this statement themselves, when describe SMAP and PSM datasets in appendix C. 
    * “This demonstrates that the main challenge in time series anomaly detection is not the representation, but rather finding the correct classifier without supervision.” – or one may say that with better representation any decent classifier would work. In fact the next sentence does exactly this, says that with the better representation those simple methods that didn’t work with the first representation now work.
    * Exp. 1. “while the raw data is not linearly separable, DPW features are able to linearly separate” – if they were able to linearly separate they would have achieved 100% accuracy. 
    * Section 5. “as windows that are well separated in time are roughly independent” – quite arguable statement as what about seasonal time series for example? 
    * Section 5. “Given the above analysis, we conclude that the average of the features of all window in a time series approximately follows the Gaussian distribution” [The main theoretical justification of the method] – the above analysis is rather vague and imprecise. As discussed above the IID assumption is quite questionable, moreover, the Central Limit Theorem also states that the Gaussian distribution is achieved only when the number of samples are infinite. Of course, in practise we can observe the distribution close to Gaussian much earlier, but no further explicit empirical evidence is provided in the paper on that. Only the exp 2 and 3 are used as evidence. 
    * Section 5, last sentence. “… distance does not admit a simple Gaussian interpretation… and therefore was not used for time series anomaly detection” – Presence of a Gaussian interpretation is not required for anomaly detection, therefore, this statement looks a bit odd.
2. General presentation issues:
    * Missing references in second paragraph of introduction
    * Missing details how window level accuracy is computed. Do the dataset have labels on the level of a particular time moment? From the rest of the text it seems that only the whole time series has a label.
    * Section 4. Exp. 1. “with 10 scales (s=10)” – s was introduced as a scale index, i.e., 10 scales would mean s \in {1, …, 10}, whereas s=10 would mean “with a scale equal to 10” [i.e. a single scale]. Which one is needed here?
    * Table 4 is wrongly referenced in Exp 1, 2 and 3.
    * Data for Exp 2. “We used the smaller datasets … ” – firstly, it seems that tables 1 and 2 contain the same set of datasets. Secondly, why for the first experiment it was possible to deal with memory requirements for the larger datasets and for the second experiment it becomes impractical apparently. 
    * Exp 3 is missing details on “multiple adjacent windows” – how many?
    * Section 5. “constant shrinkage factor” – missing reference
    * Section 6.1. Results. “GOAD and NeuTraL achieved the best performance of all the baselines” – wrong statement. GOAD is outperformed by other baselines on all the datasets.
    * Section 6.2. Benchmark paragraph. It was called Datasets in Section 6.1
    * Section 6.2. Benchmark. “(so dimension r=54 in total)” – r was used before for the dimension of the projection.
    * Section 6.2. Baselines. The name ST-GCAE should be connected with Markovitz et al somewhere for the Baselines paragraph to make sense with the table 4. 
    * Section 6.3. Baselines. Never in the previous text the names of the conferences were mentioned for the related work.
    * Section 6.4. Number of projections – What is the number of bins? What is the type of the projections?
    * Appendix B. Missing reference to Table 8. Missing details on how these error bounds were computed. 
3. Unclear statements:
    * Window-level anomaly scoring. I am a bit confused here. First, score(a) is computed assuming \alpha_w = 1/n, but then we pretend \alpha_w is not a constant when we take a derivative over it? 
    * Window-level anomaly scoring paragraph. “One interpretation…” – Why would the hyperplane have this vector?
    * Section 6.1. Dataset. “UEA datasets (obt)” – what is (obt)?
    * Section 6.1. Results. “It also … is well-grounded” – What does it mean?
    * Section 6.2. Benchmark. “Each observation…” – does it mean that the experiment is not trying to find anomalies for an individual person?
    * Section 6.3. Metric. What is point-adjust?
4. Typos/missing words/other minors:
    * Missing year in SVDD reference
    * Section 2. Second paragraph, 4th sentence. “This representation was also used by ” – missing reference apparently
    * Section 3. First paragraph. s is called a stride and a scale. Better to stick with one name for it.
    * Section 3. “Discertized” -> Discertized
    * Section 3, before eq (1). “The resulting projected matrix” – a vector?
    * Section 3, last paragraph. “maximal and minimum” – to be consistent it is better to use either “maximal and minimal” or “maximum and minimum”
    * Table 2. “single win” is not immediately apparent to correspond to single window
    * “OCC” acronym is not defined
    * Section 5. First sentence. “series series”
    * Section 5. 3rd sentence. “aa” -> “a”
    * Section 5. Paragraph starting with “We propose…”. Sentence starting with “While a the windows” -> “a” is redundant
    * Section 5. Method. “By taking the logarithm and neglecting the constant term,” – of what?
    * Section 6.1. Metric. “we USE the series”
    * Section 6.2. Benchmark. “as Markovitz et al. Markovitz et al.”
    * Section 6.2. Metric. “provided by the dataset” -> “provided in the dataset”
    * Section 6.3. Baselines. “in ICLR’22” -> “at ICLR’22”
    * Section 6.3. Baselines. “SMDSu et al.” – missing blank
    * Section 6.4. Effect of Gaussian density estimation. “but instead the [?] of each dimension”
    * Section 6.4. Effect of Gaussian density estimation. “We compare [WHAT?] using…”
    * Section 6.4. Effect of Gaussian density estimation finishes with two “. .”
    * Section 8. “making finding an accurate classifier even without supervision [POSSIBLE?]”
    * Appendix F. “Analysis in Sec ??”
    * Appendix G. Lee et al reference is missing a year.
    * Appendix H. “anomaly detection can be USED”
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity**: On the high-level the paper is easy to follow and I liked this empirical inspiration used before the formal method formulation, but as listed above, the paper does not look polished enough and this in fact the main weakness of the paper. 

**Quality**: The method is very simple (and does look sound). I don’t find theoretical justification too convincing. It is not required, so I would suggest just downplaying it in the text. The empirical part looks good. I find it a bit odd that in Section 6.1 all the results for baselines were only copied from one paper. Hopefully, the authors ensured the fair comparison. 

**Novelty**: Despite its’ simplicity the method appears to be novel.

**Reproducibility**: It seems that all the details are present but as mentioned below, some of them would be worth mentioned in the main text, not only in the appendix. 

Other comments/suggestions (these don’t impact the score):
1. Section 2. Last sentence of the first paragraph. “These approaches were originally developed for image anomaly detection” is followed by a single reference. As there are many works on image anomaly detection, I suggest adding “e.g.” for this reference or add more references. Otherwise, it suggests that this reference is unique.
2. The fact that the method uses the setting where there are N time series appears for the first time in Section 3. There are time series anomaly detection tasks aimed to detect anomalies within a single time series. Therefore, it is worth mentioned earlier what kind of settings is assumed in this work.
3. The notation section implies that all training time series have the same length T. Considering that the resulting method uses the average of window features, it seems it should tolerates time series of different lengths. If this is true, it would be better to discuss this. If it is not true, this limitation (that training time series have to be of the same length) should also be discussed.
4. Section 3. I would suggest putting the sentence “Prior to window extraction…” before the preceding sentence to avoid confusion about why the number of windows should be equal to the length of the time series and how is it possible for any \tau > 1.
5. Section 3, “Discertized projection” paragraph. P \in R^{(d \dot T \dot s \times r)} looks confusing. It is better to introduced a variable for dTs.
6. Table 1. It would be helpful if anywhere it would be introduced that “EPSY”, “NAT”, etc are the names of the datasets.
7. Section 5, first paragraph. “at the window level, BUT/HOWEVER/ETC it is …”
8. Section 5, around eq. (3). It would be good to have a couple of words connecting the anomaly score and likelihood.
9. Section 6.3. Some more details how the projection features work for windows of length 1 would be appreciated.
10. Section 6.4 should be moved at the beginning of the Section 6 and should be finished with something like: “in the next experiments we used our model with 100 random projections and 20 bins”. – this would avoid questions about the settings before a reader has a chance to read until Section 6.4. And what about the scale? Was it not tested? I appreciated that the implementation details are given in the appendix, but since it is already discussed in the main text, there is a better place to have it.
content.summary_of_the_review:
It is quite an intriguing paper suggesting very simple method which appears to outperform the complex deep learning methods. Because it is so unusual it would probably be helpful to have even more empirical evidence (but the current version is ok), especially with Section 6.1 experiments where the results for baselines were only copied from another paper. But this is just a suggestion for improvement, and it does not affect scoring too much because there is a much bigger issue with the current submission – its’ unreadiness for publication (see details before). I am not sure the time available for revision of the paper during this review process would be enough to fix all the issues. 

Moreover, this issue is so big that it is difficult to assess the others. For example, that absence of intuition behind projected features mentioned above looks rather insignificant in comparison to the presentation issues, but once the presentation is fixed, it would be possible to assess other aspects and may be this absence of intuition would look more significant. 

All in all, I am suggesting rejection of the paper in its current form as it is not ready for publication, however, I would like to see this idea published eventually as it is quite intriguing that such a simple method may outperform those giant deep learning methods. 

**Question to authors for rebuttal**: What is the intuition behind the projected quantized features?

content.title: Window Projection Features are All You Need for Time Series Anomaly Detection
content.TL;DR: A simple hand-crafted representation combined with a Gaussian estimator obtains SOTA results in time series anomaly detection.
content.abstract: The challenge of time series anomaly detection has motivated the development of increasingly more complex deep representations and anomaly metrics. In this paper we demonstrate that a simple approach based on window projection features can achieve better results. Projection features are a common way to discretize multivariate data; they first multiply the data by a projection matrix followed by discretization of each output dimension. We first show that short temporal windows, encoded by projection features, are often already sufficiently expressive for linearly separating between normal and anomalous time series. However, we find that while the expressivity of projection features is sufficient, current one-class classification methods are unable to use them effectively to detect anomalies. We hypothesize this is due to the difficulty of density estimation. The difficulty can be overcome by estimating the probability density of the sample mean, which follows the Gaussian distribution when the conditions of the Central Limit Theorem are met. Simply put, we fit a multivariate Gaussian model to the average of the projection features of adjacent windows within a time series. Despite its simplicity, our method outperforms the state-of-the-art in diverse settings including: five UEA datasets, video trajectory anomaly detection and standard anomaly segmentation benchmarks. Code is provided.
